content: Ascorbic acid, commonly known as vitamin C, is a naturally occurring organic compound with antioxidant properties. It is typically a white solid, though impure samples may appear yellowish. It dissolves readily in water, forming mildly acidic solutions. Ascorbic acid is one of the vitamers of vitamin C. Initially referred to as L-hexuronic acid, it was renamed ascorbic acid when its role in preventing scurvy (a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency) was discovered. The name ascorbic acid is derived from a(meaning no) and scorbutus (scurvy). While many animals can synthesize ascorbic acid from glucose, humans and certain other species, such as some primates, guinea pigs, bats, and certain fish and birds, require it as a dietary micronutrient. Historically, the connection between citrus fruits and the prevention of scurvy was noted as early as the mid-18th century. Initially, it was believed that the acidic properties of lemon and lime juice were responsible for this benefit, but it was later understood that other dietary acids, like vinegar, did not have the same effect. In 1907, Norwegian physicians identified a compound in food that prevented scurvy, distinct from the one preventing beriberi. Using guinea pigs as a model, they demonstrated the essential role of this compound, which was later named vitamin C. Between 1928 and 1932, Albert Szent-Györgyi and Charles Glen King independently identified the antiscorbutic factor as a specific chemical substance. Szent-Györgyi isolated hexuronic acid from animal adrenal glands and suspected it to be the antiscorbutic factor, but biological assays were needed to confirm this. In 1932, King’s laboratory proved that hexuronic acid was indeed vitamin C. Later that year, Szent-Györgyi’s team discovered that paprika peppers were a rich source of the compound. Walter Norman Haworth, a British chemist, collaborated with Szent-Györgyi to determine the correct structure of vitamin C and synthesized it in 1934. The compound was named L-ascorbic acid to reflect its antiscorbutic properties. Haworth received the 1937 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on ascorbic acid, while Szent-Györgyi was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his studies on its biological functions. Ascorbic acid is classified as a reductone, with its ascorbate anion stabilized by electron delocalization. This stabilization makes it more acidic than expected for a compound with isolated hydroxyl groups. Its antioxidant mechanism involves donating electrons, but in the presence of free metal ions, excess ascorbate can promote free radical reactions, potentially acting as a pro-oxidant in certain metabolic contexts. In food chemistry, ascorbic acid and its salts (sodium, potassium, and calcium ascorbates) are widely used as water-soluble antioxidant food additives. However, they cannot protect fats from oxidation. For this purpose, fat-soluble esters of ascorbic acid, such as ascorbyl palmitate or ascorbyl stearate, are used. Approximately 80% of the global supply of ascorbic acid is produced in China. Its European food additive E numbers include E300 (ascorbic acid), E301 (sodium ascorbate), E302 (calcium ascorbate), and E304 (fatty acid esters of ascorbic acid). Ascorbic acid also reacts with glucose and amino acids at high temperatures (90°C), producing volatile compounds. It serves as a cofactor in tyrosine oxidation. Beyond food applications, ascorbic acid is used in various niche, non-food contexts. It acts as a reducing agent in photographic developer solutions and as a preservative. In fluorescence microscopy, it enhances fluorescent signals and reduces dye photobleaching. It is also employed to remove dissolved metal stains, such as iron, from fiberglass swimming pool surfaces. In plastic manufacturing, it facilitates molecular chain assembly with reduced waste. Intravenous high-dose ascorbate is being investigated as a chemotherapeutic and biological response-modifying agent in clinical trials. Additionally, heroin users use ascorbic acid to convert heroin base into a water-soluble salt for injection. It is also used to neutralize iodine in water purification, removing the taste, color, and smell of iodine. Ascorbic acid is biosynthesized in plants and animals from glucose. In animals, it is produced in the liver or kidneys, depending on the species, via the enzyme L-gulonolactone oxidase. However, humans, other higher primates, guinea pigs, and most bats lack this enzyme due to mutations, making dietary intake of vitamin C essential. In plants, multiple biosynthesis pathways exist, often derived from glycolysis intermediates. The primary pathway involves L-galactose, which is converted to L-galactonolactone and then to ascorbic acid by mitochondrial enzymes. Ascorbic acid also plays a role in iron reduction and uptake in dicot plants. Industrially, ascorbic acid is synthesized from glucose using the Reichstein process or biotechnological methods. The Reichstein process involves catalytic hydrogenation of glucose to sorbitol, followed by microbial oxidation to sorbose. Subsequent chemical reactions yield ascorbic acid. Modern biotechnological methods use genetically modified microbes to streamline production, bypassing intermediate steps. Artificially synthesized D-ascorbic acid, while possessing antioxidant properties, has minimal vitamin C activity compared to L-ascorbic acid, highlighting the importance of the correct enantiomer for biological functions. The determination of ascorbic acid content traditionally involves titration with oxidizing agents, such as iodine, in the presence of a starch indicator. Alternative methods include back titration with sodium thiosulfate or potentiometric titration. Faraday’s law can be used to calculate ascorbic acid content. Another oxidizing agent, N-bromosuccinimide (NBS), can also be employed in titration, with the endpoint indicated by a blue-black complex formed with starch.
